data.name: Samurai of Hyuga
data.detailed_description:
Samurai of Hyuga is a brutal, heart-pounding interactive tale. Prepare to enter the land of silk and steel, where fantasy clashes against grim reality, and where the good guys don't always win in the end. It's a harsh world with tough choices at every turn. Good thing you're the toughest ronin around.

"Samurai of Hyuga" is a 135,000-word interactive fantasy novel by Devon Connell, where your choices control the story. It's entirely text-based--without graphics or sound effects--and fueled by the vast, unstoppable power of your imagination.

A bodyguard, an assassin, a savior. Become all those things and more! Will you be able to change your ways and protect those around you? Or will you succumb to your bloodthirst and become the ultimate manslayer? Will you find love, or lust? Will you adopt a code of honor, or do whatever it takes to win? Can your spirit survive against your own demons?

Combat, drama, and so much more await you in the first book of this epic series!

  • Become a badass ronin, a master manslayer, and reluctant bodyguard for hire!
  • Join with your spirit animal to take on mythological oni!
  • Face down your own demons in this dramatic, unforgettable adventure!
  •  Over 140,000 words of interactive fiction!

reviews.review:
[h1]FANFIC FOR WEEBS[/h1]

Samurai of Hyuga had been on my radar for quite some time. I was curious to find out why this particular Interactive Fiction series generates such polarizing opinions. On paper, it sounds really interesting - a fantasy setting inspired by real-world history, cool mythological elements, romantic buildup, and the option to play as a complete asshole. 
After almost five hours and finishing the first book, I finally get it. I understand why so many people either love it or hate it.

Samurai of Hyuga feels like fanfiction-level writing with a main character who too often comes across as a self-insert. You can tell there’s genuine passion behind the text, and everything makes sense in its own weird way, but I just couldn’t take anything that happened seriously (more on that later).
[b]In my opinion, this simply isn’t a good story, and I can’t recommend it.[/b] It’s a very specific game aimed at a very narrow subset of weebs and anime fans. Is that a bad thing? Hell no. If you like it, you like it. It’s just not my thing.

[b]World[/b]
If you were excited about historical Japan being the setting for this game, then I have some bad news for you. Samurai of Hyuga takes place in a fantasy land heavily inspired by Japan, but it’s not actually Japan. The game borrows various historical elements and mixes them together into this weird mumbo-jumbo. Maybe I just expected a bit too much from it?

[b]Story[/b]
Samurai of Hyuga tells the story of a ronin hired to protect a young noble child named Masashi. Unfortunately for us, it doesn’t take long for everything to go wrong, and we quickly get dragged into another mission - hunting down and killing various demons. The book ends with [spoiler]us killing the first demon from our "list", followed by an annoying cliffhanger where someone from our past tries to kill Masashi[/spoiler].
It’s not the most interesting plot in the world, but I’ve definitely seen worse. This game is first and foremost an "action-adventure" in IF form, so you should adjust your expectations accordingly.

[b]Writing[/b]
First things first: the choices and dialogue in this game can be both incredibly dumb and unbelievably cringy. You can tell the author is actually capable of writing decent prose, but he has this bizarre tendency to throw immersion-breaking modern speech into completely random places.
Random example: “I still had a chance with this exotic-looking babe.” Bro... why? And adding "baka" or "gomenasai" to the dialogue definitely doesn’t help either. Even weebs should realize that this is a bit too much, right? 
There’s also one particularly annoying moment that really stuck with me. Why even include this random option to spare a fish, only to immediately tell me afterward that this game is for mature audiences and I’m apparently not allowed to do that? Just don’t give me the option in the first place instead of pulling that kind of nonsense.

[b]Characters[/b]
You have the option to play as either a male or female character. You can also change your sexual preference, which in turn gender-swaps the romanceable options (and Masashi as well...) to match your choice.
We don’t know much about our backstory. We know we were an orphan, and that a lot of dark things happened before "now", but the game doesn’t spend too much time filling in the details (though from what I’ve seen, later books focus much more on it).
Surprisingly, the secondary characters are actually not bad, and I can see why someone might stick around for a second or even third book just to see what happens with them.

[b]Stats[/b]
Not gonna lie, the stat system in this game is just weird. It makes some sense at the beginning, when you’re defining your character through choices. For example, you can play as an unashamed pervert and get some funny dialogue, or you can be a chivalrous protector of Masashi. 
But the moment the attunement system gets introduced, things start getting annoying. It forces you to pick answers that match your character’s established personality, otherwise you lose attunement. Losing too much attunement can even lead to a bad ending. This basically kills the ability to choose dialogue purely for roleplay, because the stat system will punish you for it otherwise.

[b]Audio & Visuals[/b]
This game is purely text-based, so there’s not much to comment on in terms of audio or visuals. Still, I’ll leave my usual note for interactive fiction: even basic visuals and audio could make these games more accessible and appealing to a wider audience, similar to what Roadwarden or Wayfarer have done.

[b]Technicalities[/b]
The lack of a save system - or at least a "back to the previous page" button - is just incredibly frustrating. I can’t stress enough how much I dislike it when interactive fiction games do this. It’s all too easy to misclick on a choice you didn’t intend, especially in longer games, so give players a way to fix it.
I only noticed a few typos/missing words here and there. No bugs or other problems.
